analysis.investment_thesis: CESC is a regulated utility — explicitly excluded from the Magic Formula because regulated returns and heavy asset bases distort both earnings yield and ROIC comparisons. Even ignoring the exclusion, operating income has declined at a -1.6% CAGR over 9 years and ROCE of 11.2% is unacceptably low for a capital-intensive business.
key_strengths: Net profit has grown steadily from ₹729 Cr (2016) to ₹1,428 Cr (2025) — a reliable, inflation-beating income stream backed by a regulated franchise
OCF positive in all 5 of 5 years; utility cash flows are predictable and support consistent dividends
Regulated monopoly in its West Bengal distribution area provides demand visibility unavailable to competitive businesses
key_risks: Operating income CAGR of -1.6% over 9 years — the core power generation business is shrinking in real terms even as revenue grows 3.8% CAGR
Debt load of ₹17,978 Cr against equity of ₹12,711 Cr (D/E 1.41) is high; borrowings jumped from ₹14,544 Cr (2024) to ₹18,811 Cr (2025) — a 29% surge
Earnings yield of ~7.4% (EBIT ₹2,849 Cr / EV ~₹38,529 Cr) fails the Magic Formula threshold even if I bent the rules to include it
red_flags: Utilities are structurally excluded from the Magic Formula — regulated returns are capped and cannot produce the high ROIC my formula requires
Net profit has been essentially flat at ~₹1,400–1,450 Cr for the last 4 years (2022–2025) — no growth despite rising revenue, suggesting margin compression
Capex surged to ₹1,863 Cr in 2025 (vs. ~₹750–780 Cr in prior years), compressing FCF to ₹729 Cr from ₹1,586 Cr in 2024
analysis.detailed_analysis: EV = ₹22,732 Cr + ₹17,978 Cr debt − ₹2,181 Cr cash = ~₹38,529 Cr. Operating income of ₹2,849 Cr yields 7.4% — below my 12% threshold. ROIC is structurally capped by the regulator, ensuring this can never be the 25%+ business I look for. Utilities offer income and inflation-hedging but not the high-return-on-capital growth engines my formula is designed to identify and purchase cheaply.
